title: In 10 days, bacteria evolved to survive 1,000 times more antibiotic
body: In a study published in 2016, researchers at Harvard Medical School and the Technion filled a dish 120 cm long with bands of agar: no drug at the edges, then **10 times more antibiotic** in each band towards the middle. *E. coli* spread until a band stopped them, and stalled there until a mutant appeared that could grow in it; that mutant's descendants fanned out across the band, and the cycle repeated at the next one. In about 10 days, bacteria were growing in the middle band, with 1,000 times the dose of the antibiotic trimethoprim that had stopped their ancestors in the first band. The race had a twist: the first lineages into a new band were often not the most resistant, just the ones in the right place.

slides.prompt: Bacteria meet a band of antibiotic strong enough to stop them. What lets them carry on into it?
slides.answer: A new mutation, one band at a time
slides.detail: They stall until a mutant appears that can grow at that dose. Its descendants spread through the band, and stall again at the next one.

slides.alt: Animation of a long dish seen from above, its bands of antibiotic rising tenfold toward the middle. Glowing E. coli spread from both ends and stall at each band until mutants break through and fan out. A zoom shows a tougher mutant boxed in behind a weaker lineage.

slides.heading: Trimethoprim in each band, in multiples of the dose that stops E. coli
slides.note: The edges had no drug. Each step is 10 times the last (Baym et al., Science, 2016).

slides.heading: Not the strongest, the nearest
slides.text: Evolution on the plate was not always led by the most resistant mutants. Some highly resistant ones were stuck behind weaker lineages that had reached the front first. When the team moved trapped mutants ahead of the front, they grew where the front could not.

left.label: Trimethoprim
left.text: About 10 days to adapt across the whole plate. Mutants from the middle band needed a dose 10,000 times higher to stop them.

right.label: Ciprofloxacin
right.text: About 12 days. Mutants from the middle band needed a dose 100,000 times higher than the original bacteria did.

slides.heading: A lab arena, not a hospital
slides.text: The researchers say their giant dish doesn't perfectly mirror how bacteria adapt in the real world or in hospitals. But it's closer to the places bacteria really live than the well-mixed cultures most lab experiments use.

slides.heading: Made to teach
slides.text: The plate was built to teach evolution in a visually captivating way. The idea came from a billboard for the 2011 film *Contagion*, where glowing microbes crept across a dark backdrop to spell out its title. Read the [paper](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aag0822).

slides.question: On the plate, which bacteria usually got into a new band first?
slides.explanation: Being in the right place mattered. Highly resistant mutants could be boxed in behind weaker lineages that happened to reach the edge of the next band first.

source.label: Harvard Medical School: Bugs on Screen
